newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FBI faces crime lab criticism, other problems.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FBI faces crime lab criticism, other problems.

text.p: Trouble is mounting for the FBI, America's most powerful law enforcement agency, and its most vocal congressional opponent says the bureau is in a "mad scramble" to keep its image intact.

Director Louis Freeh has come under particular attack after serious problems at the bureau's once-vaunted crime laboratory and after the FBI failed to solve some high-profile cases and engaged in a public clash with the White House.

The controversy may escalate in the next few weeks as the Justice Department plans to release separate reports sharply criticising the laboratory's management and the handling of the initial suspect in the Olympic bombing in Atlanta, Richard Jewell, who was eventually cleared.
"The bureau is now doing a mad scramble to control the problems," Sen. Charles Grassley, a leading congressional critic, said in a Senate speech last week that blasted Freeh.
"We put too much trust in the FBI," said Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs a judiciary subcommittee that oversees the bureau. "The FBI has squandered our trust."
At a House appropriations subcommittee hearing chaired by Representative Harold Rogers earlier this month, Freeh faced similar attacks on his leadership of the 89-year-old agency.

"Your judgment in several high-profile episodes is coming under increased scrutiny and raises serious questions that have cast serious doubts about the independence of the FBI," said Rogers, a Republican from Kentucky.

He cited the FBI's naming of Jewell, a security guard at Centennial Olympic Park, as a suspect in the July 27 bombing that killed one person and injured more than 100. After a controversial investigation, in which Jewell's name leaked to the media, he was cleared in October 1996.

The Justice Department has been investigating whether FBI agents improperly tried to trick Jewell into waiving his constitutional rights after the bombing by calling him to their office on the pretext of making a training video.
Department sources said several FBI agents involved in the Jewell questioning may face disciplinary action.
Meanwhile the FBI has been stymied in solving the Olympic pipe-bomb attack as well as subsequent Atlanta-area bombings at an abortion clinic and a predominantly lesbian nightclub.

In another high-profile case, the FBI has been unable to pinpoint the cause of the July 17 explosion of TWA Flight 800. All 230 passengers and crew on board were killed, shortly after takeoff from New York City.

Relations between the White House and the FBI, strained by several earlier disputes, received another setback on March 13, when the bureau became embroiled in a public confrontation with President Bill Clinton.
The FBI contradicted Clinton's version on why he did not learn about allegations that China was considering giving money to congressional candidates. China denied the allegations.

Clinton said FBI agents at the June briefing of White House National Security Council aides insisted the information not be passed on to higher-ups, but the FBI in a statement denied placing any restrictions on dissemination.

"I would not have handled it that way," one senior Justice Department official said of the FBI statement, which had not been cleared by Attorney General Janet Reno. The FBI, as part of the Justice Department, reports to Reno.

Of all the problems facing the FBI, the most serious one has involved its laboratory, which conducts more than 600,000 examinations of evidence each year for local, state, federal and international law enforcement agencies.

A soon-to-be-finished Justice Department investigation criticised the laboratory for sloppy handling of evidence, raising questions about procedures and contaminated evidence, department officials said.
The FBI said on Thursday it "is fully committed to correcting all problems in the laboratory" and vowed to "take disciplinary action as required once the investigation is completed."
Freeh, selected by Clinton in 1993 and confirmed by Congress to a 10-year term as FBI chief, denied the bureau was in turmoil or significantly distracted by the problems.
"My morale is fine," he said during a rare meeting with reporters last month.
